Q: How to match numbers AND the parentheses that surround them using regular expressions in pyspark A:

I think there are two problems going on. First, let's look at the regexp_extract function call in SQL:

regexp_extract(descr, '(\\([0-9]+\\))$')

We get a little syntax highlighting to assist with comprehension. Next, let's extract the regex and unescape the SQL special characeters so we end up with a raw regular expression:

(\([0-9]+\))$

You can see the outer parentheticals are capturing the entire string: (123) because the inner parentheticals are escaped: \([0-9]+\). The outer parentheticals are used to capture a chunk of the string, but I think you really want the inner parentheticals to capture the digits. This changes the regex to:

\(([0-9]+)\)$

Now, the entire regex matches (123), and the inner parentheticals capture the digits inside. Converting this back to SQL, we need to escape the \ characters again, giving you:

regexp_extract(descr, '\\(([0-9]+)\\)$')

The regexp_extract function takes a third parameter called idx, which is the index within the match group that should be returned. The docs don't specify a default value for the third parameter, idx, but I bet it's returning index zero, if omitted. For the regex you have, you'll get the following match groups:

[0]: "(123)"
[1]: "123"

You'll also likely need to supply 1 as the idx param to extract just the digits, making the final SQL:

    with c as (
        select 1 as id, 'test (123)' as descr --want to match
        union all
        select 2 as id, 'test 123' as descr --the match I do get but don't want
        union all
        select 3 as id, 'test (884)' as descr --want to match
        union all
        select 4 as id, 'work.test' as descr
        union all
        select 5 as id, 'work(999)test' as descr
    )
    select id, descr, regexp_extract(descr, '(\\([0-9]+\\))$', 1) as extraction
--                                            ^^       ^^    ^^^
    from c
    where regexp_like(descr, '\\(([0-9]+)\\)$')

But I think we have one more problem to address: the SQL is written as a string literal in Python, and I don't think you have enough backslashes. You'll notice in the raw SQL above, I'm using \\ — the \ character is an escape character in SQL, too, so in a SQL string literal, \\ is treated as a plain old \ character, not an escape sequence. The Python string literal, having only two backslashes, means SQL gets a single backslash, making \\ in Python an escape sequence in SQL.

Vexingly, you need \\\\ in your Python string literal for SQL to get \\.

The resulting Python code should be:

df = spark.sql("""
     with c as (
        select 1 as id, 'test (123)' as descr --want to match
        union all
        select 2 as id, 'test 123' as descr --the match I do get but don't want
        union all
        select 3 as id, 'test (884)' as descr --want to match
        union all
        select 4 as id, 'work.test' as descr
        union all
        select 5 as id, 'work(999)test' as descr
    )
    select id, descr, regexp_extract(descr, '\\\\(([0-9]+)\\\\)$', 1) as extraction
    from c
    where regexp_like(descr, '\\\\(([0-9]+)\\\\)$')
""")

df.show()

Aside: at some point it's worth considering storing non-trivial queries as .sql files, and then loading their contents to execute the query so you don't need to escape the escaped escapes. You'll get proper SQL syntax highlighting as well, making problems like this easier to spot in the future.

Q: Is it good practice to store GlobalKeys in Bloc state to scroll a chat list to the newest message? A:

You're mixing layers. Keys are view layer, bloc is model layer. Bloc data should have no idea about the views.

Q: JPA Logging Level on Glassfish v3 Server A:

Long answer for Sorro's comment

With the following setup you can change log level in Payara Micro on the fly without restart by help of property enableDynamicLogging. Payara Server should be similar. Setup also respects EclipseLink parameter and transaction logging.

persistence.xml

<persistence version="3.0" xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_3_0.xsd">
  <persistence-unit
    name="db"
    transaction-type="JTA">
    <jta-data-source>java:global/datasource</jta-data-source>
    <properties>
      <property name="eclipselink.logging.parameters" value="true"/>
    </properties>
  </persistence-unit>
</persistence>

This is much less config than said in https://wiki.eclipse.org/EclipseLink/Examples/JPA/Logging or any other Internet source you find. Hence EclipseLink log level properties and property eclipselink.logging.logger is not needed. You can use the same persistence.xml in Arquillian.

logging.properties

handlers=java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler
java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler.formatter=com.sun.enterprise.server.logging.ODLLogFormatter
com.sun.enterprise.server.logging.ODLLogFormatter.ansiColor=true
java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler.level=INFO

org.eclipse.persistence.level=FINER
my.package=FINER

This is Payara default logging.properties appended by EclipseLink and own code stuff.

build.gradle

...
def loggingProperties = layout.projectDirectory.file("logging.properties").asFile.path

test {
    ...
    systemProperty("java.util.logging.config.file", loggingProperties)
}

payaraMicro {
    environment 'payaramicro_logPropertiesFile':loggingProperties,
            'payaramicro_enableDynamicLogging':true
    ...
}
...

Other build tools analogous.

Dockerfile

FROM payara/micro:6.2025.7-jdk21

ARG LOGGING_PROPERTIES="logging.properties"

WORKDIR $DEPLOY_DIR
COPY --chmod=644 build/libs/app-*.war .
COPY --chmod=644 $LOGGING_PROPERTIES .
RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' $LOGGING_PROPERTIES
RUN ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sed -i -e 's/.level=INFO/.level=${ENV=LOG_LEVEL}/g' $LOGGING_PROPERTIES"]

WORKDIR /opt/payara

ENV payaramicro_logPropertiesFile=$DEPLOY_DIR/$LOGGING_PROPERTIES
ENV payaramicro_enableDynamicLogging=true

Having ENV stuff by default in logging.properties can not be handled by gradle test task. The ENV value is taken from docker compose env file and can not be changed without upping again. Hence if you want to change log level in container on the fly define log level directly in logging.properties in container.

Payara supports some kind of relaxed binding like Spring. Meaning Java system property names are mapped to environment variables names.

Q: Insert data from one SQL table to another table using Insert statement A:

You need to convert columns into rows and back into columns. That seems a good case for PIVOT

SELECT
    uniqueid_c,
    [1] AS Discipline1_c, 
    [2] AS Discipline2_c,
    [3] AS Discipline3_c            
FROM @tb_cdsa_eligibility 
OUTER APPLY (

    SELECT [1], [2], [3] FROM (
        SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY pos) AS position, val FROM (
                      SELECT 1 pos, CASE WHEN slp_c = 'Y' THEN 'SLP' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 2 pos, CASE WHEN ot_c = 'Y' THEN 'OT' ELSE NULL END val 
            UNION ALL SELECT 3 pos, CASE WHEN SpecEd_c = 'Y' THEN 'SE' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 4 pos, CASE WHEN medical_c = 'Y' THEN 'MED' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 5 pos, CASE WHEN pt_c = 'Y' THEN 'PT' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 6 pos, CASE WHEN sw_c = 'Y' THEN 'SW' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 7 pos, CASE WHEN psych_c = 'Y' THEN 'PSY' ELSE NULL END val
            UNION ALL SELECT 8 pos, CASE WHEN other_c = 'Y' THEN 'OTH' ELSE NULL END val
        ) AS allDisciplines 
        WHERE val IS NOT NULL
    ) AS notNullDisciplines
    PIVOT (
        MAX(val) FOR position IN ([1], [2], [3])
    ) AS pivotTable

) AS pivotedDisciplines
ORDER BY uniqueid_c;
